12.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "chordoma"
- Say → "AP X-ray of the pelvis and axial computed tomography (CT) of an older adult. There is a **midline sacral, osteolytic** lesion with **ill-defined** margins. The cortex shows **destruction** with a large anterior **soft-tissue mass** and **matrix calcification**. So this is a **malignant** lesion."
- Then → "In this age and site my differential is **chordoma**, giant cell tumour, chondrosarcoma, metastasis, myeloma. Next I would ask for **magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the whole sacrum and spine**, staging, then a CT-guided core biopsy in line with the resection."

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **50–60 · midline sacrum and clivus · destructive mass with calcification · physaliferous cells, brachyury · wide resection ± radiotherapy**

### 1 Definition
- Chordoma → **malignant** · notochordal origin; slow-growing, locally destructive

### 2 Origin
- Tissue → **notochordal** remnants · benign notochordal cell tumour → link to chordoma debated, transformation not proven

### 3 Incidence
- **Age** → median **57 years** (OKU (Orthopaedic Knowledge Update) Tumors 4) · general rule · **Sex** → male, up to **3 : 1** (Campbell)
- **Relative incidence** → Rank → **commonest primary malignancy of the sacrum**; 2nd primary spinal malignancy after myeloma (Campbell)

### 4 Sites
- **Longitudinal** → the two **ends of the spinal column**: sacrococcygeal >50% · skull base >30% · mobile spine ≈10% (Campbell)
- **Transverse** · **Special sites** · Never → **midline**, vertebral body; most sacral tumours **below S3**; never in the limbs

### 5 Clinical presentation
| Local | Systemic | Complications by location |
|---|---|---|
| Low back or gluteal pain for >1 year; **mass on rectal examination** | None | Sacrum → radiculopathy (30%), constipation, bladder = advanced (OKU Tumors 4) · skull base → headache, cranial nerves |

### 6 Imaging
**X-ray**

| Frame A step | Textbooks |
|---|---|
| Site · Behavior | Sacrum, vertebral body · osteolytic, sclerosis in 64% (Greenspan) |
| Margins · Cortical reaction | Destructive, scalloped · both cortices destroyed, large soft-tissue mass |
| Special signs | **Calcification in >50%** (necrosis, not matrix) (Campbell) |

- Plain film often missed → **lateral sacral view**; bowel gas hides it · **MRI** = most useful → low T1, very bright T2; lumbar-only MRI misses it (Campbell)
- **Bone scan** → normal or reduced; cold centre

### 7 Labs
- **Routine** → Basic labs only; no specific test

### 8 Biopsy
- **Modality** → **Core biopsy** planned with the surgeon · gross → lobulated, **gelatinous** · microscopy → cords in **myxoid** stroma, **physaliferous** ("bubble-bearing") cells
- Markers → S-100 + keratin + **brachyury** (specific) · types → classic · chondroid (15%, skull base, better) · dedifferentiated (poor) (OKU Tumors 4)

- Chordoma histology: physaliferous cells in a myxoid background (PMC7961966, CC BY)
- Chordoma destroying the sacrum and L5, sagittal specimen (Greenspan)

### 9 Differential diagnosis
| Method | Chordoma |
|---|---|
| **Location groups** → By location | Midline sacrum → chordoma, giant cell tumour (GCT), chondrosarcoma, metastasis, myeloma |
| By cortex | Destructive with a soft-tissue mass, not expansile |
| **Histology groups** → By cell | Physaliferous, brachyury → no giant cells, no small round cells |
| **Special DD** → The mimic | Benign notochordal cell tumour → sclerotic, cortex intact, no mass |

### 10 Grading
- **Enneking** + American Joint Committee on Cancer (**AJCC**) → 2 Work-up; most chordomas **low grade**

### 11 Treatment
- **Margin** → **Wide en bloc resection**, even at the cost of a neurological deficit · **Systemic** → chemotherapy → no proven benefit (Campbell)
- Margin not wide, contaminated or unresectable → **radiotherapy** (protons, carbon ions)

CLINICAL PEARL — the S3 rule
- Both **S3 roots kept** → near-normal bowel and bladder · both **S2 roots** cut → complete loss (Campbell)

PITFALL — "resection + radiotherapy" for every chordoma?
- Handbook, Greenspan → always radiotherapy · Campbell, Miller → only if the margin is not wide. Say → "**wide resection; radiotherapy if the margin is not wide or unresectable**"

### 12 Prognosis & complications
- **Prognosis** → Survival → 73.5% at 5, 58.7% at 10 years (OKU Tumors 4) · metastasis <5% at presentation, **30–60% later** (Campbell)
- Worse → >5 cm, positive margins, metastases · better → young, distal sacral tumour

- **Two sites?** → sacrococcygeal and skull base (ends of the column)
- **Cell?** → physaliferous cells; brachyury
- **Treatment?** → wide resection ± radiotherapy; chemo-resistant

12.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "adamantinoma"
- Say → "Lateral X-ray of the tibia of an adult. There is a **diaphyseal, cortical, mixed** lesion with **well-defined** margins in the **anterior cortex**. The cortex shows **expansion**. **Soap-bubble** loculation. So this is a **malignant** lesion until proved otherwise."
- Then → "In this age and site my differential is **adamantinoma**, osteofibrous dysplasia, fibrous dysplasia. Next I would ask for **MRI** to see the medulla, then an **open biopsy**."

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **20–40 · anterior tibial diaphysis · soap bubble, sawtooth cortex · epithelial nests, keratin + · wide resection only**

### 1 Definition
- Adamantinoma → **malignant** (low grade) · unknown origin; malignant **epithelial** cells in fibro-osseous tissue · classic or **osteofibrous dysplasia-like**

### 2 Origin
- Aberrant epithelial nests → subcutaneous bone · some see it as the malignant end of **osteofibrous dysplasia** (OFD) → OFD-like adamantinoma → classic

### 3 Incidence
- **Age** → classic mean 35 · OFD-like mean 14 · OFD <15 (OKU Tumors 4) · **Sex** → male = female (exception) · **Relative incidence** → Rank → 0.1–0.5% of primary bone tumours

### 4 Sites
- **Longitudinal** → **diaphyseal** · **Transverse** → **cortical, anterior**
- **Special sites** → **tibia 85–90%**, fibula too in 10–50% (OKU Tumors 4) · Never → outside long bones

### 5 Clinical presentation
| Local | Systemic | Complications by location |
|---|---|---|
| Pain for years; anterior **bowing**; mass; prior trauma in half | None | **Pathological fracture ≈20%** (Campbell) |

12.03.l: Bone Tumours — Rare Malignant Tumours, Soft-Tissue Sarcoma & Pathological Fractures
12.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "lymphoma of bone"
- Say → "AP X-ray of the humerus of an adult. There is a **metaphyseal and diaphyseal, central, osteolytic** lesion with **ill-defined (permeative)** margins. The cortex is largely **intact** with little periosteal reaction. So this is a **malignant** lesion."
- Then → "A patient who feels well with a large lesion makes me think of **lymphoma**; differential Ewing sarcoma, myeloma, metastasis, osteomyelitis. Next I would ask for **MRI** for the soft-tissue mass, staging with positron emission tomography–CT (PET-CT) and marrow biopsy, then a **core biopsy sent fresh** for flow cytometry."

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **>40 (6th–7th decade) · femur, pelvis, spine · permeative, big soft-tissue mass, ivory vertebra · small round cells, CD20 · chemotherapy + radiotherapy**

### 1 Definition
- Primary lymphoma of bone → **malignant** · haematopoietic · one bone ± one node, nothing else for 6 months (OKU Tumors 4)

### 2 Origin
- Lymphocytes → most are **diffuse large B-cell** non-Hodgkin · Hodgkin → rarely starts in bone; bone = stage IV

### 3 Incidence
- **Age** → **6th–7th decade** · general rule · **Sex** → male 1.5 : 1 · **Relative incidence** → Rank → ≈3% of primary bone malignancies (OKU Tumors 4)

### 4 Sites
- **Longitudinal** → **diaphyseal** often (Campbell) or metaphyseal (OKU Tumors 4) · follows red marrow
- **Special sites** → **femur** commonest, then pelvis, spine, ribs (Campbell)

### 5 Clinical presentation
| Local | Systemic | Complications by location |
|---|---|---|
| Rest and night pain; **lesion large, symptoms mild** | Usually none; patient feels well, unlike myeloma | **Pathological fracture** · spine → hidden in "osteoporotic" collapse |

### 6 Imaging
**X-ray**

| Frame A step | Textbooks |
|---|---|
| Behavior | Osteolytic; sclerotic less often, and after treatment |
| Margins | **Permeative or moth-eaten**; well-defined border extremely rare |

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Adult (child → rhabdomyosarcoma) · deep thigh · >5 cm, deep, growing · spindle or round cells · wide excision + radiotherapy**

### 1 Definition
- Soft-tissue sarcoma (STS) → **malignant** · mesenchymal tissue near bone (fat, muscle, nerve, vessel); usually respects fascia

### 2 Origin
- Mesenchymal · pre-existing lesions → **neurofibroma (NF1) → MPNST** (malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour), radiation → more aggressive

### 3 Incidence
- **Age** → adults; **15–20% under 15 years** (OKU Tumors 4) · **Relative incidence** → Rank → adult **UPS**, then **liposarcoma**; children → **rhabdomyosarcoma** · <1% of cancers

### 4 Sites
- **Longitudinal** → **proximal thigh**, pelvis → large before found · **Transverse** → **deep to fascia** in 70–75% (OKU Tumors 4)

### 5 Clinical presentation
- **Local** → Red flags → **>5 cm · deep to fascia · growing** → sarcoma until proved otherwise (Miller) · recurrence after an outside excision
- Pain does **not** separate benign from malignant · often **painless** → wrongly called lipoma · small long-standing → synovial, epithelioid, clear-cell

### 6 Imaging
- **X-ray** → Plain film first → calcification (synovial), ossification, bone erosion; often only a soft-tissue bulge
- **MRI with contrast** for any mass >5 cm or deep → low T1, high T2, heterogeneous, necrosis
- **CT** → **Chest CT** for all; CT abdomen–pelvis for **myxoid liposarcoma** · PET-CT not routine

| **Synovial sarcoma** | 15–40 | Knee, **foot** (commonest foot sarcoma) | t(X;18); calcification 25–30% (Greenspan); not from synovium | + radiotherapy; chemosensitive |
